title: Empirical Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Loop for Intent→Network Configuration Using a Deterministic Reachability Validator
abstract: We measure the marginal effect of wrapping a single LLM generator (declared gpt-5-mini) with a deterministic reachability validator plus at most one automated repair (a GVR loop) on intent→device-configuration tasks. Using a preregistered paired shared‑initial design (cns-m2026-01) with N=300 intents (600 episodes), the baseline generator produced execution‑validated correct configurations in 299/300 tasks (99.667%); the guarded pipeline (validator ± one repair) produced 300/300 (100.0%). Paired difference = 0.00333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap‑percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Provider-call accounting: 301 model calls (300 generator calls + 1 repair call). All model calls, validator traces, scoring JSON, manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes to enable reproducible reanalysis; representative artifact paths and SHA values are cited in the Disclosure Statement and in-text. We discuss operational implications, threats to validity, and reproducibility procedures grounded in the archived execution artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed as intent→configuration proposers in NetOps automation (translate operator intent into device commands). A common operational architecture adds a deterministic validator (reachability/policy checker) in front of execution and, if needed, an automated repair step to correct unsafe or non‑executable outputs. Prior work describes architectures and prototypes for LLM‑assisted network configuration and verifier‑assisted loops, but there is limited preregistered paired empirical measurement of the marginal effect of such a gate on real execution validation outcomes with full archival of model calls and validator traces.

We evaluate the concrete research question preregistered as cns-m2026-01: Does an LLM generator wrapped by a deterministic reachability validator plus at most one automated repair increase the paired rate of correctly executable, intent‑satisfying configurations compared to the same generator alone? Our contribution is a fully preregistered, evidence‑archived paired experiment (shared‑initial semantics) with deterministic task selection, closed‑world emulator validation, exhaustive provenance (per‑call provider traces), and transparent statistical analysis. All archived artifacts (model responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSON, manifests, and hashes) are enumerated in the execution manifest and analysis outputs and are referenced throughout.

Key empirical outcome summary (reported unchanged from archived analysis): baseline successes = 299/300 (0.996667); guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0); paired difference = 0.003333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Provider calls used = 301 (one repair invocation only). These precise numbers and the analysis logs are archived (see Disclosure Statement and Analysis Artifacts).
sections.related_work:
Nearest work and positioning. Recent NetOps and AIOps literature explores intent translation, verifier‑assisted pipelines, and generate–validate–repair architectures (e.g., intent→config benchmarks and verifier pipelines). Representative engineering and research leads that motivated our protocol include NetConfEval‑style intent translation studies and verifier‑assisted synthesis prototypes (see cited_record_ids). Prior studies often report prototype success rates but omit preregistered paired designs, full per‑call provenance, or deterministic validator traces. Our run differs by: (1) preregistered paired shared‑initial protocol (isolates marginal gate effect), (2) deterministic emulator reachable‑state validation and explicit validator trace per episode, (3) archival of every model call and scoring artifact with SHA‑256 for reproducibility.

Evaluation practices and threats in LLM measurement are widely discussed in contemporary LLM evaluation surveys; we follow their recommendations: preregistration of estimands, contamination filtering of public data, fixed RNG seeds, and archival of all intermediate artifacts (see pledged artifact manifest).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and high‑level design. The study was preregistered (cns‑m2026‑01). The preregistration froze: research question, paired shared‑initial design, contamination/exclusion criteria, retry policy, repair budget (≤1 automated repair call), confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided), and bootstrap CI plan (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Preregistration SHA‑256: 0726a6c02c1ed6fc379927f4bb0696330f0b00484f15caee5cf4ebc072316bf7 (archived manifest). The master prompt (initial prompt that directed the autonomous researcher) is archived and referenced below (Disclosure Statement).

Task bank, selection, and contamination controls. We assembled a 300‑intent corpus using (i) filtered publicly available intent→configuration candidates and (ii) deterministic synthetic intent templates to meet preregistered strata. The automated selection pipeline performed deterministic contamination checks (exact string and k‑token shingle overlap) and excluded items above thresholds; inclusion/exclusion rules and the final task manifest are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl — SHA‑256 cited in Disclosure). The shared‑initial semantics were used: the same single generator proposal (one text candidate per intent) was evaluated under both experimental conditions (baseline and guarded) to isolate the gate's marginal effect (preregistered design).

Generator, validator, and guarded pipeline. Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json — SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The guarded pipeline ran a deterministic reachability validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that parses the candidate configuration into typed commands, simulates device‑state transitions in a closed emulator snapshot, enforces task constraints (allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, final_group_constraints), and reports any unintended reachability or policy changes. If the validator rejects the candidate, the pipeline allowed exactly one automated repair call (the preregistered repair budget). All validator traces and scoring JSON were archived per episode. The transformation and emulator snapshot identifiers are recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 archived).

Execution contract and provider accounting. The run followed the preregistered contract: task_count = 300, planned_episode_count = 600, maximum_model_calls = 600, retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient infra failures, and missingness rules (exclude pairs where both conditions cannot be executed). Actual completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301 (300 generator calls + 1 repair call). The full provider‑call traces and per‑call cache entries are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/call_cache/ (manifest and SHA‑256s available).

Scoring and confirmatory analysis. Episode outcome: binary (1 = execution‑validated configuration that satisfies intent and produces no unintended reachability changes; 0 otherwise). Primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test comparing discordant pairs (n10, n01). Complementary uncertainty quantification: bootstrap‑percentile 95% CI for paired difference (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Analysis was executed by the registered analysis executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1'; analysis logs and artifacts are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl — SHA‑256 cited). All per‑episode scoring JSON files (execution/scoring/*.json) contain validator traces, normalized configurations, and scoring rationales.

Reproducibility and archival. To enable exact reproduction we archived: raw model responses (execution/responses/*.txt), per‑episode scoring JSON (execution/scoring/*.json), provider‑call traces (execution/provider_calls/*.json), call cache (execution/call_cache/*), task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), transformation manifest, model configuration, and a complete execution manifest with SHA‑256s and timestamps. Representative artifact SHA‑256 values are included in the Disclosure Statement and in the execution manifest. The preregistered analysis settings and seeds (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729) are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary numbers. Planned episodes = 600 (300 intents × 2 conditions). Completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider‑call accounting: model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generator calls + 1 repair call). Per‑condition aggregated outcomes (analysis/condition_summary.csv — archived): baseline successes = 299/300 (0.996667); guarded successes = 300/300 (1.0).

Primary confirmatory statistics (archived analysis). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) shows n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 (registered exact test implementation; see analysis log). Bootstrap‑percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). These exact values, the contingency CSV, and the analysis log are archived and their SHA‑256 values are listed in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.

Representative examples and forensic artifacts. We include three representative per‑episode artifacts (one from each early task) to illustrate validator traces and normalization: pair‑000001 (task‑000001), pair‑000002 (task‑000002), and pair‑000003 (task‑000003). Each episode's shared initial proposal, baseline execution scoring, and guarded scoring JSON files are archived (execution/responses/* and execution/scoring/*) and contain the deterministic validator trace (parsed commands, simulated final states, violation lists). For example, execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...) is identical to both baseline and guarded proposals for that intent; the per‑episode scoring JSON records validator decisions and normalized configurations. The single repair that changed the paired outcome is archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json (SHA‑256 cited in Disclosure) and is traceable to a single repair invocation.

Statistical interpretation. The observed paired improvement is small (0.00333 absolute) because the baseline generator was near ceiling on this controlled emulator corpus. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 reflects the small discordant counts (n10=1,n01=0) under the prespecified exact two‑sided test; the bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01] captures the limited uncertainty range given the results and resampling settings. The run therefore provides direct empirical evidence that a deterministic validator plus one repair can correct an isolated LLM mistake with minimal extra model call cost, but measurable aggregate gains depend on baseline error rates and validator coverage.

Exploratory artifacts. The repair‑iteration histogram (Figure 1) and failure‑mode breakdown (Figure 2) are generated from the archived scoring JSON files; they show 299 tasks needing zero repairs and 1 task needing a single repair. The failure‑mode taxonomy (validator violation, syntax/parse, execution/emulator mismatch, and specification ambiguity) is annotated by the per‑episode scorer and archived (analysis artifacts). No residual guarded failures remain, so H2 (plurality of residual failures are specification ambiguity) cannot be confirmed in this run because the guarded condition left zero failures.
sections.discussion:
Operational implications. Practical NetOps pipelines can benefit from a deterministic validator with modest repair budgets: the architecture corrected an isolated generator failure at small additional cost (one repair call) and with full auditability via validator traces. However, when generator accuracy is already very high on the target distribution (near ceiling), the observable aggregate effect will be small; operations teams should weigh validator coverage, repair budget, and expected baseline error rates before deploying a gated GVR loop in production.

When a larger practical effect is required, candidates include: (1) increasing repair budget (iterative repair); (2) expanding validator checks (deeper runtime emulation, multi‑device semantics); (3) using the guard only for critical changes rather than all proposals; or (4) applying the gate on more difficult or higher‑risk intent strata. Any such change must be empirically evaluated; our archived artifacts enable reanalysis with alternative decision rules or simulated larger repair budgets without re‑running the LLM calls (provider calls are archived for the single repair observed, but not for hypothetical extra repairs).

Threats to validity and limitations (detailed). Internal validity: the shared‑initial design isolates the gate but differs from pipelines that regenerate a new proposal per condition; our choice was preregistered and documented. Construct validity: we operationalized safety as absence of emulator‑observed unintended reachability changes within the closed snapshot; this is a useful but partial proxy for real production risk. External validity: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a deterministic emulator limit generalisability; results do not imply equivalent outcomes for other LLMs, broader corpora, or live production devices. Conclusion validity: the ceiling baseline shrinks power to detect large improvements and makes null hypothesis testing less informative for large‑effect targets; the exact test and bootstrap CI are reported transparently.

Reproducibility and forensic utility. Every model response, provider call, scorer JSON, and analysis log has been archived with SHA‑256 and can be examined to reproduce the reported findings. Key artifact paths and hashes include: execution/raw_results.jsonl (176776d1...), task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl — 91564bb6...), per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json), per‑call provider traces (execution/provider_calls/*), and the repair trace for the lone repair (execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json — 4deb410d...). The registered analysis executor produced the exact McNemar p and bootstrap CI; its run parameters and seeds are logged (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl — 7db06f53...). These artifacts permit independent reanalysis and alternative statistical computations without re‑issuing model calls (except potential additional repair calls not executed).
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired shared‑initial experiment (cns‑m2026‑01) that measured the marginal effect of adding a deterministic reachability validator and ≤1 automated repair to a single LLM generator for intent→configuration tasks (N=300). The guarded pipeline corrected one isolated baseline failure at the cost of a single repair call; baseline success = 299/300, guarded success = 300/300, paired difference = 0.00333, exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). The practical conclusion is constrained: verifier‑assisted repair can fix isolated LLM mistakes with low extra cost, but demonstrable aggregate benefit depends on the baseline error rate, validator coverage, and repair policy. All execution artifacts, per‑episode traces, and analysis logs are archived with SHA‑256 to enable reproducible reanalysis and extension by other researchers.

disclosure_statement:
Disclosure Statement — archived provenance and runtime facts

Initial master prompt immutable reference (archived): provenance/master_prompt.txt — SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba.
Preregistration: cns‑m2026‑01 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 0726a6c02c1ed6fc379927f4bb0696330f0b00484f15caee5cf4ebc072316bf7). The preregistration froze the paired shared‑initial design, contamination/exclusion rules, retry policy, repair budget (≤1), confirmatory exact McNemar two‑sided test, and bootstrap CI plan (10,000 resamples, seed=1729).
Declared LLM(s) and model identifier: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json — SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). Provider traces and per‑call cache are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and execution/call_cache/ (full manifest indexed in execution/execution_manifest.json; representative provider‑call repair trace: execution/provider_calls/task‑000117‑guarded‑repair.json — SHA‑256: 4deb410d5736ab332cd5caaf00b16051e5b0aef2276255c0770098f63cb523ba).
Orchestration and tools: adapter_family 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' orchestrated generator→validator→(optional repair). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0); transformation and emulator‑snapshot identifiers are listed in execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 archived). Execution used shared‑initial semantics (single generator proposal per intent reused in both conditions) as preregistered.
Artifact archival and reproducibility: every model response, provider‑call trace, validator trace, per‑episode scoring JSON, and analysis output is archived with SHA‑256. Representative artifact SHAs: raw results execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 176776d1...), task manifest execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 91564bb6...), per‑episode example execution/responses/task‑000001‑shared‑initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...), analysis paired table analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = 3421adb5...), analysis log analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 7db06f53...). The registered analysis executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1' produced the reported McNemar p‑value and bootstrap CI; its run parameters and seeds are logged (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). 
Autonomy boundary and human roles. The Research Director selected the topic family and approved the master prompt before the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock the AI autonomously performed literature review, gap selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, artifact archiving, statistical analysis, manuscript drafting, AI‑based peer review, and revision. No manual technical edits of the manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsals existed but were not used as empirical evidence; all reported empirical results derive from the archived autonomous run only.
Limitations (short): ceiling baseline, single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini), closed‑world emulator validator proxy, single‑repair budget. Full limitations and per‑artifact references appear in the manuscript body.
limitations: Ceiling baseline: baseline success = 299/300 reduces power to detect large preregistered improvements.
Task scope and external validity: deterministic emulator‑backed intent corpus; results do not directly generalise to noisy, adversarial, or human‑authored intent distributions in production.
Model scope: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini); no cross‑model generality claimed.
Validator construct validity: safety operationalised as absence of emulator‑observed unintended reachability changes in a closed‑world snapshot; production safety surfaces may be broader.
Repair budget: only a single automated repair attempt was permitted; iterative multi‑call repair strategies were not evaluated in this confirmatory run.
